## Why 18 State Attorneys General — Republicans and Democrats Alike — Wanted CLARITY Dead

URL: https://chainbrief.news/state-ags-federal-preemption-clarity-act
Published: 2026-09-17
Section: Regulation & Policy

Buried under the ethics fight and the stablecoin lobbying was a quieter, more technical objection that cut across party lines entirely: a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general warned the bill would let crypto fraud defendants argue their way out of state court.

Most of the coverage of the CLARITY Act's failure focused on the ethics fight over the Trump family's crypto business, or the stablecoin-rewards dispute between banks and crypto firms. A quieter objection got less national attention despite coming from an unusually bipartisan coalition: eighteen state attorneys general, led by New York's Letitia James and including Republican Kris Kobach and Democrat Rob Bonta among the signatories, sent the Senate a letter urging it to reject the bill outright over federal preemption. The core claim: "qualified transaction" The AGs' objection centers on a specific phrase in the bill's text: its definition of a "qualified transaction." Their letter argues that definition would let the SEC's federal framework preempt state securities and commodities enforcement over transactions that would otherwise fall under state authority — meaning a state attorney general trying to bring a fraud case against a crypto platform could find a defendant arguing that federal law already occupies that ground, regardless of whether the SEC actually brought its own case. The "reserved" language fig leaf More recent drafts of the bill added language the AGs describe as "reserving" certain state fraud-prosecution powers — an attempt to address exactly this concern. The coalition's response was that the reservation language is too vague to rely on in practice: as the letter put it, they "remain firmly opposed to any federal statutory changes that would displace states' authority to oversee the securities and commodities markets," arguing that ambiguous statutory language is precisely the kind of thing that reads fine in a press release and collapses the first time a well-resourced defendant's legal team tests it in court. “We remain firmly opposed to any federal statutory changes that would displace states' authority to oversee the securities and commodities markets.” — from the eighteen state attorneys general’s letter to the Senate The stakes they cited The letter leaned on FBI figures putting crypto-related fraud losses at $11.4 billion in a single year to argue for why the preemption question isn't academic. State attorneys general have historically been among the more active enforcers against crypto fraud targeting their own residents, often moving faster than a federal agency juggling a national caseload — losing that tool, even partially, is the concrete harm the coalition says it's trying to prevent. Why the bipartisan makeup actually matters Most of the CLARITY Act's fault lines split cleanly along industry-versus-critic or party lines. This one didn't. Attorneys general don't agree on much when it comes to crypto policy broadly, but protecting their own office's enforcement authority against federal preemption is a structural, institutional interest that cuts across party — a Republican AG in one state and a Democratic AG in another both lose the same tool if the preemption language is written badly, regardless of their party's general posture on crypto regulation. What happens to this concern now The CLARITY Act's stalled status means the preemption fight is paused, not resolved — the underlying drafting concern doesn't go away just because the bill isn't moving. It's also the kind of narrow, technical fix that's genuinely well-suited to the amendment process a successful cloture vote would have opened, rather than a reason to sink the entire bill on its own. If CLARITY or something like it comes back, expect the "qualified transaction" language to be one of the first things renegotiated — it's a fixable problem, not an irreconcilable one, and the eighteen AGs who signed this letter have already told the Senate exactly what a fix would need to look like.

## The SEC Just Let Real Stocks Trade on Public Blockchains

URL: https://chainbrief.news/sec-tokenized-stocks-exemptive-relief
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Markets & On-Chain

A five-year exemption lets tokenized U.S. shares trade on automated market makers on Ethereum, Solana, and BNB Chain without those venues registering as exchanges. Companies get 30 days' notice and a veto before their stock shows up.

On September 17, the SEC granted a five-year exemptive-relief framework that lets tokenized U.S. stocks trade directly on automated market makers (AMMs) — decentralized trading venues that price assets algorithmically instead of matching buy and sell orders the way a traditional exchange does — running on public blockchains including Ethereum, Solana, and BNB Chain. The venues don't have to register as securities exchanges to do it. This isn't the synthetic "stock token" model some platforms have offered for years, where a derivative tracks a share's price without conferring any actual ownership. The SEC's order requires real shares, carrying real dividend and voting rights, represented on-chain. How the exemption actually works Exemptive relief is a specific SEC tool: rather than writing a new rule through the full notice-and-comment process, the agency uses existing statutory authority to exempt a defined activity from requirements that would otherwise apply — in this case, exchange registration. It's the same general mechanism the SEC has used before to let novel financial products operate ahead of, or instead of, a full rulemaking (spot ETFs are a familiar example). That makes this framework flexible and fast to issue, but also less durable than a statute: a future SEC could narrow or revoke it without needing Congress. The guardrails The relief isn't unconditional. Trading venues have to notify a company 30 days before its shares begin trading on-chain, and the company can object and block participation — an issuer veto that doesn't exist for ordinary secondary-market trading of a stock today. Venues also have to run know-your-customer (KYC) checks, apply trading limits, and layer permissioned access controls on top of what are otherwise open, permissionless blockchains. In practice, that means the underlying settlement layer is public, but who can actually trade isn't — a hybrid that regulators clearly designed to keep AML and investor-protection obligations intact rather than exporting them to code. Who's positioned to benefit — and who's shut out Tokenization platforms including Securitize, Bullish, Superstate, Dinari, and Fairmint are positioned to build the compliant rails this framework requires. Coinbase and Robinhood, both of which already run brokerage infrastructure, are expected to have a head start adapting to it. DeFi trading venues like Uniswap, Aerodrome, and Raydium are the AMMs this relief was written for in the first place. Notably excluded: the synthetic products that already exist. Robinhood's earlier Stock Tokens product and Kraken's xStocks track share prices without granting real ownership, dividends, or voting rights — exactly the model this exemption doesn't cover. Ondo's offshore tokenized-equity products fall outside it for similar reasons. If those platforms want to operate inside this new framework, they'd need to rebuild around real, custodied shares rather than price-tracking derivatives. “This gives a way to trade real tokenized stocks,” Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo said, calling it a step that will “accelerate adoption of native tokenized security.” Why this is the same story as the CLARITY Act, again This is the fourth piece we've covered in the past week of regulators moving on their own after the Senate failed to pass the CLARITY Act: the SEC and CFTC's earlier pledge to act with or without Congress, Circle launching its own permissioned blockchain, and now an actual exemption letting real securities trade in DeFi. None of it required a single vote in the Senate. Whether that's a pragmatic way to keep U.S. markets competitive while Congress sorts itself out, or a workaround that leaves Wall Street's newest market structure resting on the discretion of whichever administration is in charge, is exactly the durability question we raised in our cloture explainer — and it applies here just as directly. What to watch The 30-day notice window is the first real test: does any major company actually exercise its veto and block its own shares from trading on-chain, and if so, why? Coinbase and Bullish shares both jumped on the news — Bullish reportedly around 10% and Securitize around 14% — which tells you the market is pricing this as a genuine new revenue line, not a symbolic gesture. Whether trading volume on the AMMs themselves follows is the harder, slower question. Further reading CoinDesk: SEC opens door to tokenized U.S. stock trading — here's who could benefit Northeast Times: SEC's tokenized-stock rule could give Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle a head start

## The CFTC Sent Its Crypto Rulebook to the White House. Here's What That Actually Means.

URL: https://chainbrief.news/cftc-sends-crypto-rules-white-house
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Regulation & Policy

Three days after the Senate failed to pass the CLARITY Act, CFTC Chair Mike Selig submitted a market-structure proposal for federal review — the clearest sign yet that Washington's crypto regulators plan to write their own rules regardless of what Congress does next.

On September 18 — three days after the Senate failed to clear cloture on the CLARITY Act — the CFTC submitted a new crypto market-structure proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review. It's a procedural step, not a finished rule, but it's a meaningful one: it confirms the CFTC isn't waiting on Congress and is moving through the rulemaking machinery it already has. What "sent to OMB" actually means Federal agencies don't just publish a new rule the moment they write one. A "significant" regulatory action typically goes through interagency review — commonly through OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs — before the agency can formally propose it. After that review, the CFTC's own reporting indicates the proposal returns to the agency for a commissioner vote, then a public comment period, then another vote before it can take effect. In plain terms: this is an early step in a multi-stage process, not a rule taking effect next week. What's actually in the proposal — and what isn't public yet The specifics haven't been disclosed. It's not yet public which crypto assets the proposal would cover, what registration or disclosure requirements exchanges would face, or how far the CFTC is reaching under its existing authority over commodity derivatives. That's worth naming plainly rather than guessing at: the headline here is that the CFTC moved, not yet what it decided. “The CFTC is locked in and ready to ship its rules for the new frontier of finance,” CFTC Chair Mike Selig said following the submission. A second, smaller move the same week Separately, the CFTC issued no-action relief allowing certain passive software providers — including crypto wallet interfaces — to connect users to regulated derivatives markets without registering as introducing brokers. It's a narrower move than the market-structure proposal, but it points the same direction: the agency easing its own registration requirements where it can, rather than waiting for new statutory categories from Congress. How this connects to the SEC's own moves This lands the same week the SEC granted its own exemptive-relief framework letting tokenized stocks trade on public blockchains. Both agencies said back in mid-September, right after the CLARITY Act's cloture vote failed, that they'd advance crypto rules independently rather than wait on legislation. This is what that pledge looks like in practice: two regulators, moving on parallel but separate tracks, using the authority they already have rather than the jurisdictional lines a statute like CLARITY would have drawn for them. Why that still isn't the same as a law The distinction we raised in our cloture explainer applies here directly. A CFTC rule, once finalized, is binding — but it's also revisable by a future CFTC under a future administration, the way guidance is, in a way an act of Congress generally isn't. Industry groups that have spent years asking for CLARITY-style legislation have said as much publicly: rulemaking is useful and can move faster than Congress, but it isn't the durable, harder-to-unwind clarity a statute would provide. That tension doesn't go away just because the agencies are moving. If anything, it's the whole reason this is worth watching rather than treating as a substitute for the bill that didn't pass. Further reading CoinDesk: CFTC sends crypto rules to White House to review as Congress stalls on CLARITY Act Jenner and Block: SEC and CFTC issue joint interpretation on crypto asset classification

## Twenty-One of the World's Biggest Banks Are Building Their Own Stablecoin

URL: https://chainbrief.news/banks-launch-joint-stablecoin-venture
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Payments & Adoption

Bank of America, Citi, Goldman Sachs, Deutsche Bank, UBS, and at least sixteen more institutions are forming a company to issue a dollar stablecoin by 2027 — a direct answer to Circle and Tether from the banks stablecoins were originally built to route around.

Twenty-one banks and financial institutions have committed to forming a joint venture that will issue a U.S. dollar stablecoin, with the company itself targeted for incorporation in the second half of 2026 and a market launch in the first half of 2027. Among the institutions named so far: Bank of America, Citi, Goldman Sachs, Deutsche Bank, UBS, Santander, Wells Fargo, MUFG Bank, Fidelity Investments, and Standard Bank. The remaining participants haven't been publicly identified. What we actually know Not much, yet, beyond the timeline and the bank list. The announcement didn't name the venture itself, its ownership structure, its executives, or which blockchain it plans to build on — only that products will be "available on public blockchains." That's an unusual amount of ambiguity for a group this large to announce publicly, and it's worth reading as a group staking a claim to the idea before the operational details are settled, rather than a fully formed product launch. Why now The consortium says it intends to comply with the U.S. GENIUS Act — the federal stablecoin framework that set reserve and licensing requirements for dollar-pegged tokens — and the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation, where applicable. That's the same regulatory backdrop we described in an earlier piece on stablecoins becoming financial infrastructure rather than just a crypto-trading convenience. The difference this time is who's building the rail. Non-bank issuers like Circle and Tether built the first generation of dollar stablecoins largely outside the traditional banking system. A 21-bank consortium is the incumbents deciding to own that infrastructure themselves rather than keep watching non-banks capture the fee-generating layer of payments they used to control. The Circle parallel This lands roughly a week after Circle launched Arc, its own permissioned layer-1 blockchain built around USDC, with a validator set that includes BlackRock, DTCC, Mastercard, and Visa. Different companies, same underlying instinct: institutions that need settlement certainty are increasingly choosing to build or co-own the infrastructure rather than plug into an existing crypto-native rail they don't control. A bank-owned stablecoin and a bank-adjacent blockchain are two different bets on the same premise — that the next phase of stablecoin adoption runs through institutions that already hold regulatory licenses, not around them. The euro token and beyond The consortium has said a euro-denominated token is the next priority after the dollar product, with eventual ambitions toward other Group of Seven currencies. That's a meaningfully larger ambition than a single U.S. dollar stablecoin — it reads as banks trying to build multi-currency settlement infrastructure for themselves, not just compete with USDC on one axis. What to watch The real test isn't the announcement — it's whether this stablecoin actually displaces volume from USDC and USDT, or simply adds another option that mostly gets used for bank-to-bank settlement rather than the broader payments and remittance use cases where existing stablecoins have real traction. We'll also be watching for the entity's name, its governance structure, and which blockchain it chooses — all still undisclosed as of this writing. Further reading The Defiant: 21 financial institutions commit to joint stablecoin venture CoinMarketCap: 21 major banks plan stablecoin venture with dollar token launch in 2027

## A Hacker Drained $319 Million From a Bitcoin Network, Then Gave Most of It Back

URL: https://chainbrief.news/liquid-network-320-million-exploit
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Markets & On-Chain

Liquid Network, a Blockstream-built settlement layer used by more than 80 exchanges, halted all transactions after a software bug let someone mint bitcoin that didn't exist. The attacker returned 85% of it after Blockstream patched the flaw — and kept the rest.

On September 6, an attacker exploited a bug in Liquid Network — a Bitcoin sidechain built by Blockstream that more than 80 exchanges and infrastructure firms use as a faster settlement layer — to mint roughly 4,000 bitcoin that weren't actually backed by any reserve, then withdraw about $319 million of it through an approved trading platform called SideSwap. The whole sequence, from the first malformed transaction to the payout leaving the network, took about 36 minutes. How a sidechain works, and how this broke it Liquid issues a token called L-BTC, meant to be backed one-to-one by real bitcoin held in a multi-institution reserve called the federation wallet — the idea being that L-BTC settles faster than bitcoin's own base chain while staying redeemable for the real thing. The bug lived in Elements, the open-source software Liquid runs on: nodes cache the results of range-proof checks, a cryptographic step that verifies a transaction's amounts are valid, to save on repeated computation. A flaw in that caching let at least one invalid output pass as already-verified — effectively letting the attacker mint L-BTC without putting up real bitcoin behind it. Blockstream confirmed this was a software bug, not a stolen private key or a breached wallet. The conditional return The attacker communicated on-chain, describing themselves as a "whitehat" and telling Blockstream, in effect: fix the bug first, and the money comes back once the fix is confirmed. Liquid halted all transactions while the federation worked on a patch. After it shipped, the attacker returned about 3,400 BTC — roughly 85% of what was taken, worth about $272 million — and kept the remaining 598 BTC, worth around $47 million. “Please fix the bug first... Then we will transfer the money back safely after confirming the fix,” the attacker wrote in an on-chain message. What's still unresolved Blockstream hasn't detailed how it plans to cover the roughly $47 million shortfall the attacker kept, or when full redemptions will fully resume for L-BTC holders. Reconstructions of the federation's reserve after the returned funds put the implied backing ratio somewhere around 86% against outstanding L-BTC — not fully reconciled, and not the one-to-one peg the token is supposed to guarantee. Liquid has since resumed operations. Why this matters beyond one sidechain This is a useful, concrete counterweight to a week of otherwise upbeat regulatory news — the SEC's new tokenized-stock exemption, the CFTC's own rulemaking push, a 21-bank stablecoin venture all landed the same stretch of days. None of that changes the fact that a settlement network used by major exchanges ran on software with a caching bug nobody caught until it cost $319 million. Regulatory clarity and infrastructure security are different problems, and this week is a reminder that solving one doesn't solve the other. Whether "whitehat" conduct after the fact should change how anyone thinks about the underlying failure is a fair question worth sitting with, not an answer this piece is trying to supply. Further reading CoinDesk: $320 million bitcoin exploit hits Liquid Network — hacker makes conditional offer TRM Labs: 2026's biggest hack to date — attackers drained $319M from Liquid Network, then returned 85%

## Crypto's Midterm War Chest Now Has AI and Sports Betting Money Behind It

URL: https://chainbrief.news/crypto-midterm-spending-2026-update
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Regulation & Policy

We covered crypto's $206 million CLARITY Act push earlier this month. New reporting puts combined crypto, AI, and sports-betting super PAC spending on the 2026 midterms at more than half a billion dollars — with Fairshake alone still holding roughly $130 million to spend.

Earlier this month, we covered the roughly $206 million crypto industry groups had pushed toward passing the CLARITY Act — money spent on a bill that failed its Senate cloture vote anyway. New campaign-finance reporting puts that figure in a bigger frame: crypto, AI, and sports-betting super PACs have combined for at least $294 million in spending tied to the 2026 midterms specifically, as part of a broader $517 million in corporate political spending on House and Senate races since January 2025 — against a backdrop of roughly $11.6 billion expected in total political advertising across the cycle. Crypto's war chest, updated Fairshake, the crypto industry's flagship super PAC funded by Coinbase, Ripple, and Andreessen Horowitz, started this cycle with $193 million and still holds roughly $130 million unspent — a reminder that the CLARITY Act loss didn't drain the industry's political capacity, it just meant the money didn't buy the outcome this round. Andreessen Horowitz's co-founders have also made personal donations of $4 million apiece, mostly directed to MAGA Inc., separate from Fairshake's own spending. New money at the table: AI and sports betting What's changed since our earlier piece is how much company crypto now has. Leading the Future, an AI-industry super PAC, has raised $140 million; Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed nonprofit, raised $100 million, including a $40 million contribution from Anthropic itself. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife have personally donated $25 million to MAGA Inc. Sports-betting operators — DraftKings, FanDuel, Fanatics, and bet365 — have combined for $72 million, largely routed through affiliate PACs like American Conservative Fund and American Future. Polymarket, the prediction-market platform, contributed $1 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund. “The scale of corporate spending in this election cycle is unlike anything we've seen previously,” said Rick Claypool, research director at Public Citizen. Where it's actually landing The clearest precedent for what this money can do is the 2024 Ohio Senate race, where crypto-backed spending helped defeat incumbent Sherrod Brown. More recently, a New York City House primary saw two Democratic candidates receive a combined $23 million from competing AI-industry groups in a single month — a race one campaign-finance researcher described as "basically two AI groups having it out with each other," with the candidates themselves treated as secondary to the fight. Why this connects back to CLARITY Fairshake's calculus going forward reportedly hinges on how individual senators voted on cloture: industry sources have said they need a recorded vote before deciding whether to concentrate spending against Democrats who blocked the bill or continue backing a bipartisan mix of crypto-friendly lawmakers. With the SEC and CFTC now both moving on their own crypto rules — see our coverage of the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption and the CFTC's rulemaking push — the industry has less urgent need for a legislative win before November, which could change how aggressively this money gets deployed in the campaign's final stretch. ## What Is "Exemptive Relief," and Why Is the SEC Using It Instead of Writing New Rules?

URL: https://chainbrief.news/what-is-exemptive-relief-sec-explainer
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Regulation & Policy

The SEC didn't pass a law or even finish a formal rulemaking to let tokenized stocks trade on public blockchains. It granted an exemption — a decades-old tool, and a faster one, with a real tradeoff attached.

When the SEC let tokenized U.S. stocks trade on public blockchains this month, it didn't do it by passing a law, and it didn't do it through a full formal rulemaking either. It used something called exemptive relief — a tool that's been part of securities regulation for decades, and one that's showing up constantly in crypto policy coverage right now without much explanation of what it actually is. The basic idea Securities law bars certain activities by default unless an exception applies. Exemptive relief is the SEC using authority Congress already gave it — typically under specific provisions of the securities and investment-company statutes — to grant an exception for a defined activity, usually with conditions attached. It's not the agency ignoring the law; it's the agency using a tool the law explicitly built in for situations that don't fit neatly into existing categories. How it's different from a full rulemaking A formal SEC rule normally goes through notice-and-comment rulemaking: the agency proposes a rule, the public gets a window to submit comments, the agency responds to those comments, and only then does a final rule take effect. That process is designed to be thorough, and it's also slow — often taking many months or longer for anything contentious. Exemptive relief, by contrast, can be granted directly by the Commission for a specific applicant or a defined class of activity, without the same extended public process. It trades some of that deliberative rigor for speed. Where this tool has been used before This isn't new. Some of the SEC's more consequential market structure has actually run on exemptive relief rather than dedicated legislation — exchange-traded funds themselves operated for years under a patchwork of individual exemptive orders before the SEC eventually adopted a generalized rule covering most ETFs. The pattern is familiar: a new product type doesn't fit the existing rulebook, the SEC grants exemptions to let it operate while it studies the space, and a more permanent rule sometimes follows years later — sometimes it doesn't, and the exemption regime just continues. The tradeoff nobody should skip past Speed comes at a cost: durability. A statute passed by Congress is comparatively hard to unwind — it takes another act of Congress. An exemptive order is a Commission-level decision, which means a differently composed Commission, under a different administration, can revisit it. That's precisely the distinction SEC Commissioner Paul Atkins raised when he called for "congressional action to provide more durable clarity" even as the agency's own interpretive and exemptive tools do real work in the meantime. Why it's everywhere in crypto coverage right now With the CLARITY Act stalled in the Senate, exemptive relief and similar tools have become the primary way the SEC and CFTC are moving on crypto market structure at all. It's the mechanism behind this month's tokenized-stock trading framework, and it's part of the same broader pattern we've covered in the CFTC sending its own rulebook to the White House for review. None of it requires a single additional vote in the Senate — which is exactly why it's moving faster than legislation, and exactly why it's less permanent than legislation would be. Further reading SEC.gov: SEC grants exemptive relief from certain filing requirements (example of the mechanism in use) Dimensional: Learn more about exemptive relief

Frequently asked:
Q: Is exemptive relief the same as a new law?
A: No. Exemptive relief is granted by the SEC under its existing statutory authority to exempt a specific activity from a requirement that would otherwise apply. It doesn't create new law, and a future SEC can narrow or revoke it without Congress acting.
Q: Has the SEC used exemptive relief for crypto before?
A: Yes, in a more limited form — some early crypto-adjacent products and services have relied on no-action letters or narrower exemptions. The September 2026 tokenized-stock framework is a larger, more structural use of the tool.
Q: Why not just write a formal rule instead?
A: Formal rulemaking requires a notice-and-comment process that typically takes months to years. Exemptive relief can be granted much faster, which matters when an agency is trying to respond to market developments in real time rather than waiting on a multi-year process — or on Congress.

## Real-World Asset Tokenization Just Crossed $34 Billion. Here's What That Actually Means.

URL: https://chainbrief.news/rwa-tokenization-market-state-2026
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Analysis

Tokenized equities are up 390% this year, bonds and money markets make up more than half the market, and the whole category still represents about 0.01% of the assets it's tokenizing. Both of those facts are true at once.

The tokenized real-world asset (RWA) market — bonds, private credit, real estate, commodities, and now equities, all represented as tokens on a blockchain — reached $34.18 billion in mid-September 2026, up 85.2% since the start of the year. Tokenized equities specifically are up 390.4% year-to-date, the fastest-growing category by far, helped along by the SEC's new exemptive-relief framework letting real shares trade on public blockchains. Both of those numbers are real. So is a third one that gets left out of most of the celebratory coverage: even at $34 billion, tokenized assets represent roughly 0.01% of the estimated $300 trillion in traditional assets they're theoretically capable of representing. Where the money actually is Bonds and money-market instruments dominate the category, at $18.29 billion — 53.5% of the entire RWA market — though that's still only about 0.017% of the global bond and money-market universe. Tokenized equities have grown the fastest but remain the smallest major slice in absolute terms, at $4.43 billion against a $151.9 trillion global listed-equity market — 0.003% penetration. Private credit, real estate (up 17.9% year-to-date), and gold and commodities (up 46.6%) round out the rest, each tokenizing at meaningfully different rates depending on how illiquid and opaque the underlying asset class already is — which tracks the three-question utility test we've applied to tokenization claims before: tokens tend to do real work where an asset genuinely lacked liquid, verifiable infrastructure to begin with. The gap between issuing a token and using one The more useful number in this data isn't total value tokenized — it's how much of that value is actually doing anything. Across the RWA market broadly, only about 12% of tokenized capital is active on-chain in any meaningful sense — deployed into lending markets, liquidity pools, or collateral, rather than just sitting as a static token representing an off-chain asset. For tokenized equities specifically, that "capital activation rate" sits at 7.54%, with most of the active share concentrated in liquidity pools (65.4%) and lending protocols (28.1%). Put plainly: most tokenized assets right now are tokenized and then left alone, not actively used the way the technology's proponents describe. AUM doesn't show how much capital is actually working — issuance and usage are two different numbers, and the gap between them is the real story in this data. An early but telling pattern: derivatives One data point worth watching: 58.5% of early tokenized-equity users are also interacting with perpetual futures on the same assets. That's a meaningfully different use case than "I want to own a fractional, on-chain share of a company" — it suggests a real chunk of current activity is traders using tokenized equities as one more instrument inside an already-active derivatives strategy, not new capital entering equity markets for the first time. Whether that shifts as the SEC's new framework matures, or stays a trading-desk phenomenon, is worth tracking over the next several quarters. For deeper RWA coverage Tokenization of real-world assets is a big enough beat that it has its own dedicated publication in our network — our sister site RWAToday.news covers the RWA sector in more depth and on an ongoing basis, if this is a category you're tracking closely. What to watch Growth in issuance is the easy number to celebrate and the least informative one on its own. The harder, more useful number is whether the capital-activation rate — the share of tokenized assets actually being used as collateral, in lending, or in liquidity provision — climbs meaningfully as more venues open up under frameworks like the SEC's new exemption. That's the number that tells you whether tokenization is building real financial infrastructure or mostly restating existing assets in a new wrapper. Further reading Crypto News Flash: Tokenized assets surge as equities lead next market expansion RWA market reaches $34.18B as equities surge 390.4%

## Staking Finally Showed Up Inside a U.S. Crypto ETF

URL: https://chainbrief.news/staking-etfs-go-mainstream
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Markets & On-Chain

Grayscale's Ethereum ETF became the first U.S.-listed spot crypto fund to pay out staking rewards. Canary Capital wants to take it further, with a staked SEI ETF designed to keep 90% of assets actively staked.

For as long as U.S. spot crypto ETFs have existed, they've had a structural gap compared to actually holding the underlying asset yourself: an investor holding Ethereum directly can stake it and earn a yield for helping secure the network, but a fund simply holding ETH in cold storage couldn't pass that yield through to shareholders. That gap started closing when Grayscale enabled staking for its Ethereum products in October 2025, and it became visible in dollar terms in January 2026, when the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF made its first distribution — $0.083178 per share, covering rewards earned between October and December 2025. Why this took as long as it did Staking isn't just "holding" an asset — it means locking it into a network's validation process, which introduces operational questions a passive custody arrangement doesn't have: which validator does the fund's ETH get staked through, what happens if that validator is penalized ("slashed") for misbehavior, and how does the fund handle the unstaking delay if it needs to meet redemptions. Those are legitimate structural questions, not just regulatory foot-dragging, and they're the reason staking inside a U.S.-listed ETF wrapper took meaningfully longer to arrive than the ETFs themselves. “Distributing staking rewards to ETHE shareholders is a landmark moment, not just for Grayscale, but for the entire Ethereum community,” Grayscale CEO Peter Mintzberg said. Who else has followed Since Grayscale's first distribution, other issuers — including products from Rex Shares/Osprey Funds and 21Shares — have launched their own staking-enabled Ethereum ETFs. Canary Capital has taken the idea further with a proposed staked SEI ETF, currently in amended S-1 filing stage rather than trading, designed to keep around 90% of fund assets actively staked rather than sitting idle — a meaningfully more aggressive staking ratio than a fund that merely offers staking as an option. SEI jumped as much as 16.5% on news of the filing, though it's worth being precise about what that reaction is actually pricing: anticipation of a product that hasn't launched yet, not a live fund. The tradeoff investors are actually buying A staking ETF isn't simply "the same fund, plus free yield." Staked assets are less liquid on a short timeline — unstaking isn't instant on most networks — which can affect how quickly a fund can meet redemptions during a period of heavy selling. It's the standard yield-versus-liquidity tradeoff that shows up throughout fixed income and cash management, just newly wrapped in a crypto ETF structure. None of that makes the yield fake; it does mean the product is a genuinely different risk profile than a plain spot ETF, not just the same fund with a bonus attached. Why this fits the broader pattern This is part of the same theme running through most of this week's crypto news: regulated products quietly absorbing features that used to live only in crypto-native tools. Staking has been available to anyone running their own validator or using a centralized exchange's staking service for years. What changed is that it now exists inside a wrapper institutional and retail investors already trust and already hold in ordinary brokerage accounts — the same structural shift we've been tracking across stablecoins, tokenized equities, and now yield-bearing crypto funds. Further reading The Block: Grayscale begins distributing staking rewards to Ethereum ETF investors CoinGabbar: Canary Capital files staked SEI ETF, SEI jumps 16.5%

## Wall Street Found a Way Into Prediction Markets Without Touching the Bets Themselves

URL: https://chainbrief.news/prediction-markets-etf-kalshi-polymarket
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Markets & On-Chain

A new ETF from Tema holds stakes in Kalshi and Polymarket, the companies — not the actual event contracts, which are still tangled up in SEC review. It's a workaround, and a fairly clever one.

ETF provider Tema recently launched a fund built around the prediction-markets sector's growth — with a structural choice that's more interesting than the fund itself. Roughly 15% of the fund's holdings are stakes in Kalshi and Polymarket, the privately held companies that operate the two largest prediction-market platforms. What the fund explicitly doesn't hold is exposure to the actual event contracts — the yes/no bets on elections, economic data, or other outcomes that Kalshi and Polymarket are best known for. Those remain tied up in an ongoing SEC review of whether, and how, such contracts should be regulated. The regulatory question this sidesteps Prediction-market contracts sit in a genuinely unsettled place: are they commodity derivatives regulated by the CFTC, are they something closer to securities, or are they closer to the state-regulated gaming and betting markets they resemble in function? That question hasn't been resolved, which is exactly why a fund can't simply hold event contracts directly without taking on that regulatory uncertainty itself. Owning equity in the companies is a different, better-understood legal category — regular corporate stock — even though the companies' underlying business is exactly the contested activity. Why this is a genuinely clever structure It's worth naming the mechanism plainly: this is regulatory arbitrage, not a loophole being exploited in bad faith. The fund gives investors exposure to prediction markets' growth — trading volume, revenue, user growth — without the fund itself having to take a position on how individual event contracts should be classified. If Kalshi and Polymarket's underlying business grows, the companies' value should reflect that, which is the exposure the fund is actually selling, whatever the SEC eventually decides about the contracts themselves. Why prediction markets have gotten more visible generally We referenced Polymarket and Kalshi odds directly in our own coverage of the CLARITY Act cloture vote — both platforms have become a genuine, if imperfect, gauge of how contested major policy outcomes look in real time, alongside their more traditional role in election and sports betting. That visibility is part of what's driving investor interest broadly, distinct from the specific regulatory question the SEC is weighing. What to watch The fund carries a 75 basis point fee, which is a meaningful cost for a thematic product and suggests real investor demand rather than a token entry into the category. Whether more issuers follow with similar company-stake structures — or whether the SEC's eventual decision on event contracts makes the whole workaround unnecessary by directly authorizing contract-level products — is the next thing worth watching in this corner of the market. Further reading Cryptonomist: Prediction markets ETF launch backs Kalshi, Polymarket stakes Bloomberg: How prediction markets upstaged election polls

## What's Actually Driving This Month's Layer-2 and DeFi Rally

URL: https://chainbrief.news/what-is-driving-september-defi-rally
Published: 2026-09-21
Section: Analysis

Starknet up 21% in a day. Uniswap up 25%. It's tempting to credit any one headline — but this rally is the product of at least four separate stories landing in the same two weeks, and they don't all deserve equal credit.

Layer-2 tokens — the assets tied to scaling networks like Starknet, Arbitrum, and Optimism that process transactions off Ethereum's main chain but settle back to it — and DeFi tokens broadly posted some of their sharpest gains of the year this week. Starknet (STRK) rose as much as 21% over 24 hours, Arbitrum (ARB) 25%, and Uniswap (UNI) climbed roughly 25% over the same window, with a broad DeFi index up 16%. It's tempting to point at one headline and call it the cause. The more honest answer is that at least four separate stories landed in the same two-week stretch, and they don't all deserve equal credit. Catalyst one: the Fed, and then the relief after it A Federal Reserve rate decision earlier in the week came in as a hike rather than the cut some traders had priced in, which rattled risk assets broadly, crypto included. The rally followed once that initial anxiety faded — helped by the 10-year Treasury yield slipping back under 5% and oil prices easing, both of which took some pressure off the inflation narrative that had spooked markets in the first place. This is a real catalyst, but it's a macro one — it explains why risk appetite returned broadly, not specifically why crypto, and DeFi in particular, outperformed other risk assets. Catalyst two: the SEC's tokenized-stock exemption The SEC's new framework letting tokenized U.S. stocks trade on decentralized exchanges names AMMs like Uniswap, Aerodrome, and Raydium directly as the kind of venue this relief was built for. That's about as direct a fundamental catalyst as a DeFi token can get — actual new, regulator-sanctioned volume potentially routing through these specific protocols, not just sentiment. This is the catalyst most likely to be load-bearing for the DeFi-specific portion of the rally, distinct from the broader market recovery. Catalyst three: the CFTC's parallel rulemaking push The CFTC sending its own market-structure proposal to the White House the same week reinforces the same theme: two regulators moving on crypto market structure without waiting on Congress. On its own, a proposal sent for interagency review doesn't create new trading volume — but it adds to a sentiment stack that's been building since the SEC's exemption, and markets often price coordinated regulatory momentum ahead of the specifics actually being finalized. Coverage of the rally has pointed to “mounting market optimism surrounding friendly, coordinated crypto regulations from the SEC and CFTC” as a meaningful piece of the recovery, alongside the macro relief. Which of these are actually real, and which are sentiment The Fed relief and the SEC's exemption are the two catalysts with a direct, traceable mechanism — one eases the macro backdrop for all risk assets, the other creates actual new regulator-sanctioned use cases for specific DeFi protocols. The CFTC news and the general "regulatory momentum" framing are real, but softer — they're sentiment amplifiers riding on top of the first two, not independent drivers with their own transaction volume behind them. That distinction matters for anyone deciding whether this rally reflects a durable shift or a short-term repricing that unwinds once the macro backdrop changes again. What to watch next The cleanest signal going forward is whether AMM trading volume in tokenized equities actually materializes under the SEC's new exemption over the coming weeks — that's the one catalyst here with a concrete, checkable outcome. If it does, this rally has real fundamentals behind at least part of it. If DeFi volume stays roughly flat while token prices retrace, that's a strong signal this month was mostly sentiment catching up to a friendlier macro backdrop, dressed up in regulatory optimism. Further reading CoinDesk: Layer-2 and DeFi tokens lead broad crypto advance as post-Fed-hike nerves fade
